He let go and lifted his wineglass in a silent gesture of inclusion; she did likewise with hers. They nodded at each other as though in agreement, turned, and walked back together to the couch where he’d been sitting.
“You can sit in the middle,” she said. “I’ll keep you company from my armchair here.”
He nodded again, looking mildly amused. She turned away to find a place to set her glass, and when she looked back he was already sitting, one leg propped against the table, fingers running through his hair to push it off his face.
She sat down and looked away toward the window.

He said nothing for a long time.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

He let go and lifted his wineglass in a silent gesture of inclusion; she did likewise with hers. They nodded at each other as though in agreement, turned, and walked back together to the couch where he’d been sitting.
“You can sit in the middle,” she said. “I’ll keep you company from my armchair here.”
He nodded again, looking mildly amused. She turned away to find a place to set her glass, and when she looked back he was already sitting, one leg propped against the table, fingers running through his hair to push it off his face.
She sat down and looked away toward the window.

He said nothing for a long time.

segment:
The sound of voices approached from beyond the door.
“I guess your friends are here now.”
The young man smiled and let go of her hand, stepping away toward the doorway. “Yeah,” he agreed, turning to wave at the group filing into the room behind him, and Mara watched as a figure emerged from the crowd to slap Jonah on the back.
Another face turned toward her, and she realized there was a man standing by her side again—a man who made Jonah look young. She wasn’t sure if that was an age difference or an authority difference, but it didn’t matter for the moment, as long as she stood in a place where everyone wanted her to stand.
Someone poured wine into her glass—the oldest man she could see here, older even than the man standing next to her—and then his arm fell away and she stood there alone, holding her glass, listening to the sound of other people’s conversation.

“I guess you need to introduce me to everyone,” she said, hoping it wasn’t true.
